why: I compared each verifier check's PASS and FAIL conditions with the words of its expect line. Check 1 asks only for "exit code is 1 and `$d/out` is empty". Check 2 asks for `bad config:`, the path "exactly as passed" and line 3 / column 3 "in any readable form", all taken from the expect line, with no exact wording forced. Check 3 asks for `OK`, meaning it threw and the message contains the path. Check 4 asks for `listening on 9000`, exit 0 and a deep-equal `{port: 9000}`, which is just what "returns `{ port: 9000 }`" means. Check 5 asks that npm test passes at head and that at least one test checking the path fails against base src/, matching the expect line. The stricter items (computing line/column instead of relying on Node's message, missing-file behavior, absolute-path resolution) all sit under "Advisory (not pass/fail)". No stricter test, mutation test or branch rule appears in any PASS or FAIL condition.
